name: Planner-only orchestration
description: The whole brain handles the turn: the planner decides, the tool runs through the registry and a reply is composed, with the deep runner disabled so deep requests come back unexecuted. A fresh orchestrator and scratch corpus are built per case so no case sees another's turns.
advantages: Every message gets the full planning treatment, including reads, confirms and clarifies, so it is the most capable path and the reference for quality.
disadvantages: Pays for a planning call even on a plain create. Simple requests take more turns and tokens than they need.

name: Direct tool-call ablation
description: One model call is given the quest record and the tool schemas and returns the tool calls as JSON, which the registry then executes. There is no planner and no answer step, so it is the upper bound on what the direct path alone can do for a plain edit.
advantages: The cheapest model path: a single call, no scaffolding. It shows how far plain edits can go without a planner.
disadvantages: It cannot read, answer, confirm or start a deep run, and it struggles with multi-step or ambiguous requests. It trusts one unchecked call to write, so it is not a replacement for the brain. Cheaper but cannot carry out multi-step or ambiguous requests.

name: Local file tree reader
description: Reads and greps files under one configured root using only regular expressions and directory walking, with no shell. It resolves paths through the shared containment check, skips secret-like, binary and oversize files, and returns partial hits within a wall-clock grep budget.
advantages: Fast, dependency-free and strictly read-only, with a hard boundary that the write side shares, so there is one implementation of containment.
disadvantages: Keyword and regex only, so a paraphrase misses. Huge trees return partial hits when the time budget runs out.

name: Cached live-database reader
description: Serves structured queries over a consumer-supplied fetch function through a short-lived in-memory cache keyed on collection and canonical filter. It is thread-safe so the planner's parallel reads do not hammer the store, and nothing is synced to disk.
advantages: Reads live data where it lives, with cheap repeated reads inside the window and no sync job to keep fresh.
disadvantages: Data can be stale for the length of the cache window. It maps read and grep onto queries only where that makes sense, otherwise returning an unsupported observation.

name: Parallel multi-source composite
description: Runs a list of member adapters in separate threads and merges the results: reads grouped by source and path, searches deduplicated, queries combined with source attribution, and discovery merged. For named reads it tries each member and keeps the first non-error answer.
advantages: A single adapter slot reaches every source, and one slow or failing member does not stop the others. Source attribution lets the planner cite where evidence came from. Selected because: RunnerConfig.retrieval (config_source_builders)
disadvantages: Unscoped searches are broadcast to every member, which costs more when a member is remote or paid. Merge rules are simple, so ranking across sources is not relevance-aware.

name: MCP server reader
description: Maps the discovery and read surface onto one MCP server: resources list and read for sources and sections, tools list and describe for operations, and tool calls for queries gated by an explicit allowlist. Every name is prefixed with an alias so servers never collide.
advantages: Reaches any MCP-speaking system without bespoke code, and the allowlist keeps a tool it was not granted from ever being called.
disadvantages: Search is delegated to the server so its quality varies, and plain regex search is not supported. It is read-only by design, so mutations need the separate write adapter.

name: Remote file server reader
description: Reads files on another machine through a file-serving endpoint using the planner's ordinary file vocabulary, namespaced by alias. It refuses names without its alias before any network call, does not follow redirects, caps response size and never leaks the access token in errors.
advantages: Extends the same read vocabulary to other machines with safe failure and no credential leakage, and search results can be pasted straight into a read.
disadvantages: Every search costs a network round trip and so must be scoped. It depends on the remote server being reachable and, like the local reader, matches by pattern rather than meaning.

name: Notion database reader
description: A read-only adapter over a configured set of Notion databases: list them, query rows with simple filters, read a page's properties and bounded block text, and search across rows. Auth is injected, only configured databases may be read, and only reads can be sent.
advantages: Two locks make it incapable of writing, and it grounds answers in structured team records the other sources do not hold.
disadvantages: Locates rows by title and properties rather than body text, so content inside a page is hard to find. It depends on a pinned API version and the integration's access.

name: Drive document reader
description: Lists folders and reads file text from a workspace drive (documents, sheets, PDFs, plain text) through the standard retrieval surface, with injected auth and lazy PDF support. Unsupported types and permission errors return error observations.
advantages: Brings shared documents into the planner's reach without copying them, and failures never break the loop.
disadvantages: Drive offers no search here, so the policy is to list and read, which scales poorly on large folders. PDF text depends on an optional package.

name: Chat conversation reader
description: Lists spaces, pulls recent messages and groups them into conversations by thread or space, exposing them through read, search and query, with optional pre-flight assembly. Auth is injected and failures come back as error observations.
advantages: Lets answers draw on discussion that never reached a document, and supports incremental fetch of messages since a point in time.
disadvantages: Chat is noisy, so relevance depends on good scoping, and it needs a delegated-access service identity. Reading is bounded by what the credential may see.

name: Quest API context reader
description: Queries the Quest backend for goal metadata, notes, related goals, task history, decisions and reflections, and skips Quest queries when a task is local-only. It is designed to sit inside the composite beside file and database adapters.
advantages: Gives the planner the product's own structured context, including cross-environment discovery, in one source.
disadvantages: It is keyed by goal and quest identifiers rather than by a free-text question, so it cannot be ranked on question-driven retrieval and is pinned by decision tests instead. Keyed by goal and quest ids against the Quest API, not by a question, so it cannot be driven offline.

name: Subprocess goal runner
description: Wraps any worker with the goal contract (composing the goal and brief, enforcing the turn bound, reading met versus limit) and provides the reference worker that spawns headless Claude Code with a goal directive. Working directory, binary, model and preamble are configuration, and a periodic liveness review can stop a stalled run.
advantages: Full autonomy for open-ended work, the simplest way to run, and the common contract keeps outcomes uniform. Selected because: config_resolvers.resolve_deep_runner_ladder
disadvantages: A fresh process per attempt throws away gathered context and is slow and costly for small edits. Nothing can reach it mid-run, so new user input only lands on the next attempt (the stream_json runner is the alternative that can be steered).

name: Agent-protocol deep runner
description: An opt-in alternative worker that holds a two-way session with an agent over the Agent Client Protocol, so a message can be injected into the turn that is running through a steering poll or a direct call. It never raises and turns a missing package, old runtime or wedged turn into a clear unmet result.
advantages: Mid-run steering, so late user input need not wait for the next attempt, with typed protocol instead of parsed command-line output.
disadvantages: Extra dependencies and a recent Node runtime are needed, there is more to configure, and it buys nothing when no one steers.

name: One-call fast file editor
description: Hands the model the context already gathered plus the current content of candidate files, asks for the edit in one call, and applies it in process through the file writer. It can touch only files already in context, does nothing when no candidate is found, and retries once with a diagnostic if a search block fails to match.
advantages: Roughly one round trip instead of an agent session, no startup, and a strict blast radius, with escalation as the safe default.
disadvantages: Limited to bounded edits to known files, and a weak edit relies on the goal loop's verifier to notice and escalate.

name: One-call MCP operation runner
description: Mirrors the fast editor for named operations: with forced structured output the model picks at most one writable operation from the writer's own catalogue and its arguments, the writer executes it, and a decline falls through to the next rung. It is reachable only through the deep ladder.
advantages: Cheap single call for a governed mutation, and an explicit decline value keeps it from guessing.
disadvantages: Can do only one operation and only those allow-listed, so multi-step or unlisted work escalates.

name: Subprocess runner scenarios
description: The selected reference worker driven through the common run entry with the process launch replaced by a scripted peer (exit code, output, stderr, missing binary, crash). Only the process edge is faked, and the way each outcome is reported is compared.
advantages: Zero model cost, repeatable, and exercises the real reporting code path.
disadvantages: Produces no tokens or dollars, so it cannot show cost per success, and it does not exercise real worker behaviour.

name: Agent-protocol runner scenarios
description: The opt-in protocol worker driven through the same run entry, with its single connection seam replaced by a scripted session (message chunks, a stop reason, a missing agent, a crash). The same scenarios allow a like-for-like comparison with the subprocess runner.
advantages: Shows that both workers report outcomes identically, at no model cost.
disadvantages: A scripted session cannot reveal real steering behaviour, latency or cost, and the opt-in extra must be installed to run it.

name: Goal contract rules check
description: Calls the deterministic rules of the done-standard directly: review parsing, liveness helpers, escalation, resume and envelope markers, prompt composition, met-versus-limit normalisation, and the orchestrator goal loop with a scripted runner and verifier, with the environment pinned.
advantages: Covers the logic every runner shares, with no model calls and no worker started.
disadvantages: Tests the contract, not any worker's ability to do the job, and relies on scripted runners that follow the cases.

name: Contained backed-up writer
description: Resolves every path through the same containment function the reader uses, refuses secret-like names, binary files and oversize payloads, copies the previous content to a backup outside the corpus before replacing it, and returns a result value instead of raising.
advantages: One shared boundary, small enough to audit, with recoverability that does not depend on version control. Selected because: RunnerConfig.file_writer
disadvantages: Fixed deny lists can miss unusual names, concurrent writers are unhandled, and a failed backup makes the write refuse.

name: Scratch-tree boundary check
description: Drives the production writer on temporary trees with an outside file as a sentinel, and observes whether the write succeeded, whether the outside stayed intact, the final content and whether a backup was kept.
advantages: Offline and exact, proving the boundary with real file operations and no mocks beyond the directories.
disadvantages: Covers the cases written down only, and does not test concurrency or very large trees.

name: MCP operation writer
description: Lists the allow-listed subset of a server's tools as writable operations and executes one by name through the client, refusing anything off the allowlist before the network, with alias namespacing and an audit detail on every result.
advantages: Strong guard and full auditability for each attempt, sharing a connection with the read adapter while keeping a separate policy. Selected because: config_resolvers.resolve_mcp_write_runners
disadvantages: Allowlist hygiene is on the host, and a call is not idempotent, so a retry after an ambiguous failure could repeat a mutation.

name: Fake-client allowlist check
description: Runs the production writer against a fake client at the process edge to check listing, exact tool and arguments once, aliased and bare names, refusals with zero calls, server error and dead connection.
advantages: Offline, fast and precise about what reached the client.
disadvantages: A fake client cannot show how real servers behave, so protocol quirks are untested.

name: Persistent stream-json runner
description: Holds one live Claude Code session per run over its stream-json input and output, so the person can steer, stop or pause while it works. A message is claimed only at the moment it is written to the session, so it arrives once and only for its own run; the model's replay of it marks it seen. A stop sends an interrupt and keeps the session, and a worker that ignores it is terminated and then killed after a grace period. A pause releases the process and resumes later on the same session. It keeps the live progress stream, resume, the subscription login, the usage-limit wait and the liveness review, and hands the run to the one-shot runner when the installed Claude Code cannot report an interrupt.
advantages: A message reaches the worker's next step within seconds instead of after the whole run, a stop takes effect at once and keeps finished work, a pause costs no memory while it waits, and a message that was written but not confirmed seen is handed back instead of being lost.
disadvantages: Not measured against live runs yet, so it is selected by nobody. It needs a Claude Code recent enough to answer an interrupt, a long-lived process per active run on a shared host, and its replay of a message is matched by text. The priority flag that should move work to the background did not do so in the probe, so only the default priority is used.

name: Coding agent, reach described in the prompt (today)
description: Outside work runs on the coding agent through the deep runner, and the model infers what it can reach from each effector's own description in the planner prompt (the tool catalog's when-to-use text, the host's grounding).
advantages: Built; no extra call.
disadvantages: A gap in the descriptions is filled with a plausible capability; no receipt is required before a claim of an outside act; a setting is not read before a blocker is stated.

name: Coding agent with the host reach summary and reach judge (built, off by default)
description: The host supplies a reach summary built from the same source as its grounding, and one small question on a stronger tier before planning settles whether the request lives inside the readable sources, outside them or in the world now; the verdict goes into the planner prompt as a fact.
advantages: Built; asks a fact instead of reviewing a decision; cached per turn; inert without a summary.
disadvantages: Off by default; settles reach for reads, not capability questions or claimed acts; adds a serial call before planning; measured on routing only.

name: Coding agent with one declared inventory and receipts (proposed)
description: Proposed. One inventory of environments and tools with what each can do and which setting allows it, read alike by the planner's grounding, the reach judge and the answer check; every outside act returns a receipt that a claim of the act must cite.
advantages: One source of truth; a false blocker or an invented capability becomes checkable; claimed acts become verifiable.
disadvantages: Every host must supply and keep the inventory current; each effector must return a receipt; not built.

name: Best open-source agent harness by the combined metric, with declared inventory (proposed)
description: Proposed. Several open-source agent harnesses, found by a survey, each do the outside work in place of the coding agent, inside the deep runner's goal loop and the library's context store, scope fences and write boundary, with the declared inventory and receipts; each is scored on the combined metric beside the coding agent, and the best of them is this arm.
advantages: Removes the dependence on one vendor's agent and its subscription; can read the library's own context store instead of searching for context afresh each session; the harness is chosen by measurement.
disadvantages: Each candidate must be wrapped to keep the boundary, scope fences, goal loop and spend limits; a mature coding agent may still complete more; a new dependency to track; not built.

name: Two small model verdicts when a goal is created (today)
description: On a shared quest, a small model names the likely assignee and judges doability for an AI representative.
advantages: Built; the only arm that makes the model call.
disadvantages: Not measured; its cost, time and value are unknown until the metric is built.

name: Creator keeps the goal, no model call (floor, proposed)
description: Proposed. A new goal stays with its creator unless the person assigns it.
advantages: No cost, no surprise assignment.
disadvantages: Goals an AI could have taken wait for a person; not built.

name: Lean guarded launch of the deep worker
description: The deep worker launched with the lean flags the chat provider already uses: only the built-in tools a worker needs (shell, file read, write and edit, find, search, web), the user settings kept so its write and delete guard hooks and model overrides still load, no ambient MCP servers, and the per-machine prompt sections moved out of the cached prefix. Selected by naming the profile in the environment (QAR_DEEP_LAUNCH_PROFILE); with the name unset the launch is exactly today's.
advantages: On one small file-and-command task, 57 to 60 percent less cost and about 60 percent fewer prompt tokens than today's launch with the same model, the same result and the same wall time, with the same hook guards. Same engine, same subscription, the prompt and environment byte for byte the same.
disadvantages: Measured on one task, two runs per arm, in a directory with no project context files, so the saving on a real goal is unmeasured. Drops the subagent, skill and notebook tools and the listing of installed skills, so work that relies on them fails until the profile is off; ambient MCP servers are not loaded.
